_about: Experimental protocol for Assignment 1, declared before any benchmark run. The scripts in ../scripts read this file; it is the single source of truth for sizes, repetitions, budgets and build/runtime flags.

study.research_question: How does matrix size n affect the runtime and peak memory of the same basic triple-loop dense matrix multiplication implemented in Python, Java and C on one fixed machine?
study.factor: matrix side length n (square n x n inputs)
outcomes: peak resident set size of the process
hypotheses: H1: runtime grows approximately as n^3 for every implementation (log-log slope close to 3); C and Java may exceed 3 at the larger sizes because the column-wise walk over B increasingly misses in cache and TLB.
H2: at every tested size, CPython is one to two orders of magnitude slower than C and Java, while C and Java stay within a small constant factor of each other once the JVM has compiled the kernel.

H3: peak memory grows approximately as n^2; C stays close to the 24 n^2 bytes of its three arrays, Java adds a roughly constant JVM overhead, and Python needs several times more per element because list-of-lists stores pointers to boxed float objects.
H4: the three implementations produce bitwise-identical results, because they perform the same IEEE-754 double operations in the same order (no FMA contraction, no reassociation).

algorithm.name: basic triple loop
algorithm.accumulation: scalar accumulator s = 0.0; for k in 0..n-1: s = s + A[i][k] * B[k][j]; C[i][j] = s

storage.python: list of lists of Python float objects (row-major, one list per row)
storage.java: double[][] (array of row arrays, each row contiguous)
storage.c: single contiguous row-major double array allocated with malloc, indexed as M[i*n + j]

inputs.draw_order: A first (n*n values, row-major), then B (n*n values, row-major)
inputs.file_format: raw little-endian float64, row-major, no header; n is given on the command line and checked against the file size

sizes._notes: Powers of two are interleaved with intermediate sizes (384, 768, 1536) so that cache-associativity effects specific to power-of-two strides can be told apart from the general trend. Sizes above 2048 are not attempted because of the session budget below.

measurement.timer_boundary: kernel only: the triple loop. Input loading, output allocation and JVM/interpreter start-up are outside the timed region. The kernel assigns every C[i][j], so the output buffer needs no re-initialisation between repetitions.
measurement.result_consumption: after each sample the program prints a checksum (sum of all C entries) so the computation cannot be eliminated
measurement.process_model: one fresh process per (language, n); it runs the warm-up samples and then the measured samples on the same input
measurement.run_order: n ascending, starting with the memory baseline n; for each n the languages run in the order c, java, python
measurement.warmup_rule: warmup_runs is a minimum: warm-up samples continue until at least min_warmup_seconds of warm-up work have run. A smoke test showed the first 0.2-0.3 s of a process running slower (C, n = 128: 1.42, 0.93, then a steady 0.84 ms per multiplication), consistent with the CPU frequency/core ramp of macOS. When one multiplication takes longer than min_warmup_seconds this rule adds nothing. All warm-up samples are kept in the raw data and excluded from the summaries.

batching.rule: Each sample times k back-to-back multiplications (k is recorded with every sample; time per multiplication = elapsed / k). The first warm-up uses k = 1; every later sample uses k = max(1, ceil(min_sample_seconds / t)), where t is the per-multiplication time of the most recent warm-up. Re-calibrating on every warm-up gives a JIT at least ~min_sample_seconds of warm-up work even when the first, interpreted run is several times slower than compiled code. All measured samples of a configuration share the same k.

measurement.summary: median and interquartile range (IQR) of the measured samples; every raw sample is kept

budgets.policy: Each process gets startup_slack_seconds to load its inputs and print its CSV header, then max_seconds_per_multiplication for every sample (batched samples last about min_sample_seconds by construction). The harness kills a process that misses a deadline, records the configuration as a timeout with the limit, and skips larger n for that language. The memory budget is checked after the run against peak RSS (macOS does not enforce RSS limits); the JVM heap is additionally capped by -Xmx. Timeouts and memory failures are reported as results, never given an invented time.

memory.metric: peak resident set size (maximum resident set size) of the whole process
memory.theoretical_reference: 24 n^2 bytes = three n x n float64 arrays (element storage only)
memory.limitations: Peak RSS covers the whole process lifetime (runtime, input loading, warm-up and measured samples). It is not the same as JVM heap use or Python object counts, and it includes the runtime itself, so the n = 1 baseline is reported alongside.

correctness.unit_tests: identity, zero, and hand-computed 2x2 / 3x3 cases in each language's test suite
correctness.reference: numpy.matmul in float64 (BLAS-backed), used only for checking
correctness.criterion: |C_ij - R_ij| <= atol + rtol * (|A||B|)_ij for every i, j
correctness.rtol: 2 * gamma_n, with gamma_n = n*u / (1 - n*u) and u = 2^-53
correctness.justification: Any summation order of an n-term dot product has forward error at most gamma_n * (|A||B|)_ij (Higham, Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms, 2nd ed., Secs. 3.1 and 3.5), so two correct results differ by at most 2 gamma_n (|A||B|)_ij. The bound is scaled by |A||B| rather than |C| because entries of C can be close to zero through cancellation, which makes a |C|-relative tolerance meaningless; it also covers exact zeros, so no absolute floor is needed (atol = 0). The cross-language comparison additionally expects bitwise equality (H4).

c._notes: -O2 is the fixed optimisation level. -ffp-contract=off stops clang from fusing s + a*b into an FMA (its default on arm64), keeping the same rounding as Java and CPython. No -ffast-math and no -march flags, so the reduction over k is not reassociated or vectorised.

java._notes: Default garbage collector (G1) and default tiered compilation. Warm-up samples let the JIT compile the kernel before measurement.

python.implementation: CPython 3.13 (Anaconda distribution), default build: no JIT, GIL enabled
python._notes: The implementation uses only the standard library (array module for loading); NumPy is used only to generate inputs and as the correctness reference, so it is not loaded in benchmark processes.
